outcomes.text: Explain the main ideas in Relative constructions and unbounded dependencies.
Recognise the patterns in real sentences.
Use the ideas when you read and write.

key_terms.definition: A cover term for relative clauses and fused relatives, including NP and PP types.
A clause containing an overt or covert element interpreted through an antecedent.
The expression that supplies the interpretation of a relative word or gap.
The element in a relative clause that is linked anaphorically to the antecedent.
An abstract empty position in a relative clause, co-indexed with the antecedent or relative phrase.
A relative clause containing a relative word such as who, which or whose.
A non-wh relative introduced by the subordinator that.
A non-wh relative with no relative word or that.
A relative clause integrated into the nominal it modifies, prototypically restricting its denotation.
A prosodically detached relative clause adding information about an antecedent.
The relative clause following the foregrounded element in an it-cleft.
A relative construction in which antecedent and relative clause are fused into one phrase.
The initial phrase in a wh relative, containing the relative word and any material that percolates with it.
A word such as who, whom, whose, which, where or when used in a relative construction.
The spread of a relative feature from a word to the larger phrase containing it.
A relative phrase containing more than the relative word itself, such as whose house or with which.
A relative use that delimits the set denoted by the head nominal.
A relative use that adds information without restricting the antecedent’s denotation.
A detached element related to an anchor without being a syntactic dependent.
A relative clause with an infinitival verb, such as a place to watch the procession from.
A non-finite clause with an understood non-subject element supplied by context.
A fused relative phrase headed by what, whoever or whichever and functioning as an NP.
A fused relative phrase based on where or when and functioning as a PP.
An interrogative clause asking for a value, contrasting with a fused relative.
A relation in which a gap can be embedded arbitrarily deeply inside the clause.
A gap that is licensed by another gap in the same construction.
A construction in which an elided VP is interpreted through an antecedent containing the elided material.

opening.prompt: Which expression is a fused relative?

options.feedback: It is an NP combining antecedent and relative.

options.text: the things that your father was saying
options.feedback: That is an NP with a relative clause.
That is a cleft relative clause.

opening.prompt: Which formal type is the toys you don’t want?

options.feedback: It has no relative word and no that.
It contains no wh word.
It contains no that.

opening.prompt: Which relative type is My father, who retired last year, now lives in Florida?

options.feedback: The relative is detached and adds information.
It is not part of the nominal’s restrictive structure.
It has a separate antecedent, my father.

opening.prompt: What is the relativised element in the people whose house we are renting?

options.feedback: Whose is linked to people; the whole phrase whose house is fronted.
House is part of the fronted phrase.
We is the subject.

opening.prompt: What distinguishes a fused relative from an open interrogative?

options.text: The fused relative functions as an NP or PP with no separate antecedent; the interrogative asks for a value.
options.feedback: Syntax and the surrounding predicate distinguish them.

options.text: The fused relative always contains that.
options.feedback: Fused relatives are wh type.
Open interrogatives also contain gaps.

closing.prompt: Why is that not a relative pronoun in the toys that you don’t want?

options.text: It is a subordinator; the object position is a gap.
options.feedback: That marks subordination rather than filling the object function.
The gap carries the relation to toys.

options.text: It is optional in subject relatives.
options.feedback: It is required in subject relatives.

closing.prompt: What distinguishes the suggestion that Kim made from the suggestion that Kim cheated?

options.text: The first is relative with an object gap; the second is a content clause.
options.feedback: The gap distinguishes the relative construction.
Both contain that.
Both are grammatical.

closing.prompt: What is relativised in the man who she said had won?

options.text: The subject of had won in the embedded clause
options.feedback: Who is linked to a deeply embedded gap.
Said takes the content clause as complement.
The subject is she.

closing.prompt: What is hollow about a place to watch the procession from?

options.text: The complement of from is understood as the place.
options.feedback: The head nominal supplies the missing element.
It contains watch.
The missing element is the object of from.

closing.prompt: What does unbounded mean in unbounded dependency?

options.text: The gap can be embedded arbitrarily deeply while still linked to the fronted phrase.
options.feedback: There is no grammatical upper limit.
Clause boundaries remain.

options.text: The relative word can occur anywhere.
options.feedback: The relative phrase is in the prenucleus.
